clue.text: Change for gorilla?

parts.note: small change is silver coins, the loose cash in a pocket
to be for someone is to back or support them

explanation.surface: Someone asks what money one might get in exchange for a gorilla.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Change for' reads as swapping cash; it is SILVER plus BACK. The question mark flags that the definition is a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A mature male gorilla is called this after the grey saddle of hair across its back.

clue.text: Abandon brushwood

definitions.meaning: to drop or cancel a plan

explanation.definitionFit: Informally to cancel something is to scrap it; the noun also means stunted vegetation.

clue.text: Harry's sound rock

parts.note: Harry Lime is the villain of the film The Third Man, so his name with the possessive
a tone is a musical sound

explanation.surface: A friend called Harry has a healthy, reliable state of mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sound' looks like an adjective, healthy; it is the noun TONE. Harry Lime is the character Orson Welles played in The Third Man.
explanation.definitionFit: A sedimentary rock made mostly of calcium carbonate.

clue.text: Improvised poem composed in foreign setting

indicators.note: the rearranged letters are placed inside the longer word

parts.note: extraneous means coming from outside, foreign to the matter

indicators.note: put together, so the letters are arranged afresh

explanation.surface: A poem written on the spot abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a poem written abroad; 'foreign' is a synonym for extraneous, and 'setting' just completes the picture of a surround for the rearranged poem.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoken or done without preparation, made up on the spot.

clue.text: Boarders here get smack on head

indicators.note: in a down entry, the first word sits on top of the second

parts.note: a smacker is a kiss, and buss is an old word for a kiss
the top is the head of something

explanation.surface: Lodgers get a slap on the head.
explanation.walkthrough: 'smack' suggests a blow; it is a loud kiss. 'Boarders' are people getting on a bus, not lodgers.
explanation.definitionFit: Passengers wait at this roadside point to get on a bus.

clue.text: Man at last has iced drink

definitions.meaning: a shoemaker, who works on a last, the foot-shaped form
a drink of wine or sherry with sugar and citrus over crushed ice

explanation.definitionFit: A shoe mender works at a last; a sherry version is a chilled drink.

clue.text: Leather stocking filler

the fleshy back of the lower leg, which fills a stocking

explanation.definitionFit: Calfskin is a leather; the muscle at the back of the shin is what fills out a stocking.

clue.text: Cockney's hurt and ready to explode

indicators.note: Cockney speech drops the H at the start of words

parts.note: to be hurt is to be harmed

explanation.surface: A Londoner who has been injured is about to blow up.
explanation.walkthrough: A Cockney is a working-class Londoner, whose accent famously drops initial H.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb that is primed and fused is said to be ready to go off.

clue.text: Model for a grand painter

indicators.note: to model is to shape, so the letters are formed into a new order

explanation.surface: Someone sits as a model for a thousand pounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a grand' suggests a thousand pounds, but the letters are just fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean-Honore Fragonard was an eighteenth-century French rococo artist.

clue.text: Fish-eater with fish left over uses new dish

indicators.note: in a down entry, the fish and the left are written above the animal

parts.note: the char is a fish of the trout family
the otter is a mammal that feeds on fish

indicators.note: renewed, so the letters are put in a fresh order

explanation.surface: An otter with leftover fish makes use of a new dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'left over' reads as leftovers but splits into L and a positional 'over', which in a down entry puts the fish and L above the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A cold dessert of custard or cream set in a mould lined with sponge fingers.

clue.text: Prophet in retrospect accepts test for controllers.

indicators.note: taking something in, so the reversed prophet holds the test within it
looking back, so the word for the prophet is read from its end

parts.note: a seer is a prophet who foresees events
the MOT is the annual UK roadworthiness test for vehicles

explanation.surface: A seer, looking back, agrees to sit an exam to qualify as a controller.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in retrospect' reads the prophet backwards, and 'accepts' takes the test inside. MOT is Britain's yearly car safety test.
explanation.definitionFit: Remote controls for televisions and other devices are commonly shortened to this plural noun.

clue.text: Tea cups made initially by one European region

indicators.note: holding in its hands, so the tea word encloses the other letters

parts.note: bohea is an old name for a black Chinese tea

indicators.note: the word's first letter only is taken

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone describes the teacups produced in a particular part of Europe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cups' is a verb here: BOHEA holds M (from 'made initially') and I (one), giving BOHE+MI+A.
explanation.definitionFit: This historic region of central Europe now forms the western part of the Czech Republic.

clue.text: For example, iron maiden in a Beatles broadcast

indicators.note: the cricket letter goes inside the rearranged letters
scattered widely, so the letters are thrown about into a new order

parts.note: M is the cricket scoring abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A heavy-metal band such as Iron Maiden is played on a Beatles radio show.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests the band Iron Maiden, but 'maiden' gives only M, put into the anagram of A BEATLES. A maiden is an over in cricket with no runs scored.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron is a common, non-precious metal, the kind contrasted with gold and silver.

clue.text: Publicity for tick

explanation.walkthrough: In British usage 'just a tick' and 'half a mo' both mean a very short moment.
explanation.definitionFit: A short promotional piece or campaign is a piece of publicity for a product.

clue.text: Established state of southern France

clue.text: Finish off like Figaro, extremely versatile in effect

indicators.note: only the very ends of the word are used

explanation.definitionFit: A law or rule that is operative is currently in force and producing its effect.

clue.text: One sets off with American serving up his salt

explanation.walkthrough: 'serving up' reverses GI to IG. 'his' means the American's, hence the US spelling NITER, not British NITRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that starts a fire or an explosion, setting something off.
